papers.title: Reversible fixation of microbial cells for targeted genomics
papers.abstract: Phylogeny- or activity-based fluorescent labelling of microorganisms coupled with fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) is a powerful approach to rapidly isolate cells of interest from complex communities for targeted genomics. However, the method has not been widely adopted because standard paraformaldehyde or ethanol fixation procedures hamper nucleic acid recovery and/or long-term sample storage. Here, we present dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP) as a reversible fixative for microbial cells that enables fluorescence imaging and DNA extraction and amplification for sequencing. DSP fixation is compatible with widely used fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches and bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging, and can be applied to diverse sample types, where it consistently performed as well as paraformaldehyde. Furthermore, high-quality genomes were obtained from individual and multiple bacterial cells selectively extracted from complex samples using FISH-FACS. Thus, DSP is a dual-use fixative for microbiome imaging and sequencing, improving targeted microbial genomics.

papers.title: Viral dispersal drives changes in population composition
papers.abstract: In an acute viral infection, a small seeding population expands rapidly over several orders of magnitude, then declines. This vast population growth is accompanied by spatial expansion as infection spreads to new anatomical sites within the host. Evolutionary theory predicts that spatially expanding populations experience more extreme stochastic losses of genetic diversity than spatially unstructured populations. To test this prediction in the context of viral dynamics, we evaluated the impact of spatial expansion on viral population genetic structure and assessed how modulators of viral dispersal affected this structure. To this end, we developed a means of implementing the spatial expansion of influenza A virus in cell culture and applied it to a viral population carrying a diverse genetic barcode. Across this simplified cellular landscape, we found that spatial expansion produces a patchwork of distinct viral subpopulations. We then evaluated the consequences for population structure of two modulators of viral dispersal: extracellular viscosity and a common polymorphism in the viral attachment protein. Both physical constraint and viral phenotype altered the extent of genetic bottlenecking and spatial heterogeneity that developed during expansion, indicating that environmental features and viral traits that modulate dispersal also modulate viral population composition, diversity and evolution.

papers.title: Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids interact with select gut microbes to produce bioactive metabolites found in infant gut metabolomes
papers.abstract: Gut microbes metabolize nutrients in infant diets, producing compounds that play roles in host health. Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) are an important component of infant diets, supporting neurological development and immune regulation. Emerging evidence demonstrates that gut microbes, alongside the host, participate in the metabolism of dietary lipids, highlighting an underexplored avenue for LCPUFA biology. In this work, alkyne-tagged eicosapentaenoic acid (EPAALK) was used to investigate interactions between LCPUFAs and the gut microbiota. Flow cytometry and comparative metabolomics identified gut microbial EPA interactors in the ileum of mice. Further comparative metabolomics analysis identified the conversion of EPA to N-acyl amino acids, including attachment to phenylalanine (EP-Phe) and leucine (EP-Leu). Targeted analysis of ex vivo stool cultures determined that EP-Phe and EP-Leu are produced by gut bacteria. A survey of lipid-relevant infant gut bacteria determined various flow cytometry-confirmed EPA-microbe interactions and identified Enterococcus faecalis, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, and Clostridium bifermentans as competent producers of EP-Phe or EP-Leu. Thus, both novel metabolites from diet-derived inputs and microbial producers of these metabolites were identified. Together, this highlights important microbiome-centric and mechanistic consequences of LCPUFA consumption and emphasizes that the gut microbiome may be an important consideration in targeted supplementation strategies.

papers.title: Evolutionary expansion of the bacterial ompW gene family enables functional diversification during host adaptation
papers.abstract: The outer membrane protein W (OmpW) family comprises minor porins essential for environmental adaptation and host interactions in Gram-negative bacteria. However, ompW is conventionally treated as a ubiquitous single-copy gene, masking its true evolutionary complexity. Through comprehensive phylogenetic analysis across thousands of reference genomes, we reveal that ompW is present in nearly half of Gram-negative lineages, exhibiting a patchy distribution governed by a birth-and-death model of evolution with recurrent duplications and horizontal transfer. Notably, copy number expansions concentrate in lineages associated with eukaryotic hosts, linking paralog accumulation to niche adaptation. Experimental validation in Acinetobacter baumannii reveals four distinct loci that maintain high structural conservation despite sequence divergence, yet undergo profound functional specialization spanning from baseline physiological maintenance to modulating host colonization and persistence in vitro and in vivo. These findings dismantle the single-copy paradigm, demonstrating that widespread gene family expansion and paralog diversification drive the phenotypic plasticity required for bacteria to colonize hostile host environments.

papers.title: Five decades of human H1N1 evolution reveal conserved glycan receptor specificity
papers.abstract: H1N1 influenza viruses have circulated continuously among human populations for five decades. During evolution, the hemagglutinin has accumulated amino acid substitutions in and around the receptor-binding site (RBS), mainly due to antigenic pressure, potentially altering receptor recognition and binding profiles. Here, we investigated the glycan-binding properties of H1N1 strains collected from 1977 through 2024 using ELISA, flow cytometry, and tissue histochemistry to characterize changes in receptor-binding specificity over time. Across the strains examined, we observe a recurring preference for binding 2,6-sialylated di-LacNAc N-glycans. Binding to 2,3-sialylated glycans was generally undetectable, although A/Hongkong/117/1977 and A/New Caledonia/20/1999 bind chicken tracheal tissues. Interestingly, post-pandemic H1N1 viruses fluctuate in their relative binding avidities. The responsible amino acids, in turn, have different effects in pre-pandemic HA proteins. We also report a classical egg-adapted H1N1 mutant that shows null binding across platforms. These findings highlight the contribution of RBS mutations during initial adaptation and evolution of human H1N1 influenza viruses to glycan-binding properties, which, in contrast to H3N2 viruses, never fail to bind glycans that correlate with avian erythrocyte hemagglutination.

papers.title: Gain-of-function mutations in the RodZ juxtamembrane domain promote Rod system activity in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall protects bacteria from osmotic lysis and determines their shape. In rod-shaped bacteria, the lateral wall is elongated by the Rod system (elongasome). This synthetic machine is built around the RodA-PBP2 PG synthase complex, the actin-like protein MreB, and the accessory proteins MreC, MreD, and RodZ. Notably, RodZ shares a similar domain organization with FtsN, an essential division protein that triggers PG synthesis by the division apparatus (divisome). Both are single pass transmembrane proteins that bind actin-like proteins in the cytoplasm and have largely unstructured periplasmic regions capped by small, folded C-terminal domains. We therefore investigated whether RodZ might function like FtsN in activating the Rod system. To this end, gain-of-function variants of Escherichia coli RodZ were isolated that restored growth and shape to cells producing a hypomorphic mreC mutant. Production of these RodZ variants in wild-type cells increased resistance to the MreB antagonist A22 and enhanced sensitivity to the beta-lactam mecillinam. These phenotypes have all previously been associated with Rod system hyperactivation, and we found that they were caused by substitutions in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane (JM) domain of RodZ. This domain is analogous to the N-terminus of FtsN known to promote divisome activation via its interaction with filaments of the actin-like FtsA protein. Structural modeling indicates that the JM domain of RodZ is similarly likely to associate with MreB filaments. Our results therefore support a model in which RodZ activates PG synthesis by the Rod system via a mechanism analogous to divisome activation by FtsN.

papers.title: Murine cytomegalovirus m119-118 encodes a new viral Fc receptor antagonizing host Fc receptor activation
papers.abstract: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) encode numerous immunomodulatory proteins to counteract innate and adaptive immunity. One class of immune evasion proteins is viral Fc receptors (vFcRs), which bind to the Fc region of IgG antibodies and interfere with antibody-mediated effector functions crucial for antiviral defense. Despite the established role of vFcRs in modulating antibody-mediated immunity, their contribution to viral pathogenesis in vivo remains incompletely understood. Although human CMV (HCMV) encodes four vFcRs, only a single vFcR, fcr-1 encoded by gene m138, has been identified in murine CMV (MCMV). By comparing and cloning the genomes of MCMV strains v70, K181+, and K181Perth, we identified a frameshift mutation affecting the spliced m119-118 transcript in K181Perth. This finding prompted us to investigate the function of the m119-118 gene. We show that it encodes a second MCMV vFcR, which we named fcr-2. It is structurally similar to its positional homolog in HCMV, UL119-118/gp68, and binds specifically to the Fc part of murine IgG. Deletion of both vFcRs genes from the MCMV genome resulted in substantially reduced Fc-binding to the surface of infected cells, indicating a complementary function of the vFcRs. Functional assays with viral deletion mutants further demonstrated that both proteins inhibit host Fc receptor activation in a cooperative fashion. Although an m119-118-deficient MCMV was only marginally attenuated in infected BALB/c mice, an m119-118 and m138 double mutant attained significantly lower organ titers than the m138-deficient mutant. These data suggest an important cooperative function of the two MCMV vFcRs for viral dissemination and pathogenesis in vivo.

papers.title: Exploring the antibiotic-producing capabilities of Canadian High Arctic bacteria
papers.abstract: Microbial communities in harsh environments such as the Canadian high Arctic, remain a relatively unexplored source of antimicrobial natural products. In this study, we developed a pipeline for screening and evaluating bacterial isolates cultured from 23 Canadian high Arctic soil, sediment, and active-layer permafrost samples to discover antibacterial compounds. The pipeline incorporated an undergraduate studentsourcing program and produced created a collection of over 350 bacterial isolates with preliminary antibacterial activity. Following dereplication, whole genome sequencing and secondary screening by co-culture assays, five isolates were prioritized to test crude extracts for antibacterial activity. Among bioactive crude extracts from these isolates, the Pseudomonas isolate with the most potent activity against S. aureus was analyzed. Using liquid chromatography bioactivity guided fractionation, we identified a potential bioactive compound known as koreenceine A, a compound previously only isolated from a Pseudomonas from temperate soil and involved in gene expression of other their microbial community. Here we expanded the known antibiotic activity of koreenceine A and confirmed that a {triangleup}kecBCD genetic knockout of the putative biosynthetic gene cluster significantly abrogated the antibacterial activity.

papers.title: A Third-generation Lentiviral Vector System for Flow Virometry-based Analysis of HIV-1 Env and Other Viral Envelope Proteins
papers.abstract: Individual human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) particles can differ in their envelope protein (Env) despite being genetically identical. This non-genetic diversity can influence antibody recognition and has been implicated in the formation of persistent virus fractions that escape complete inhibition by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Investigating non-genetic diversity in HIV and other viruses requires approaches capable of characterizing antibody binding to individual viral particles. Flow virometry provides a promising tool for single-particle analysis, but a system combining high biosafety with specific particle labeling and versatility is lacking. Here, we developed a third-generation lentiviral vector system specifically designed for flow virometry. Fluorescent proteins were incorporated into the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein between the matrix- and capsid-encoding regions, flanked by viral protease cleavage sites, creating the packaging constructs pLentiFlow-eGFP and pLentiFlow-mCherry. Lentiviral particles (LVPs) based on pLentiFlow vectors were fluorescent and retained infectivity comparable to LVPs generated with the parental vector system despite reduced particle production. We optimized LVP detection on a CytoFLEX nano and defined a linear p24-based concentration range for reliable single-particle analysis. Using complementary controls, we demonstrated that background from the assessed sources accounted for no more than approximately 3% of events within a broad eGFP+ gate and confirmed that the detected fluorescent particles were predominantly membrane-enclosed. As a proof of concept, LVPs were pseudotyped with vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike, or HIV-1 Env. Envelope-specific antibody binding was detected using 8G5F11, CR3022 or PGT128, respectively, demonstrating that different viral surface proteins can be analyzed on a common particle backbone. Together, these results establish a third-generation lentiviral vector system for flow virometry that combines intrinsic particle labeling with high biosafety and flexible pseudotyping. The system provides a platform for investigating envelope protein-associated non-genetic diversity and its consequences for antibody recognition in HIV and other viruses.

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

papers.title: LytM family endopeptidase LmdC is controlled by regulated auto processing and proteolytic destruction in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Enzymes that cleave the bacterial peptidoglycan sacculus, known collectively as autolysins, are critical for growth, division and morphogenesis, but their activities must be carefully controlled to avoid catastrophic lysis. Some autolysin control mechanisms have emerged, but we still know little about how most of them are regulated. Here, we report a novel control mechanism for the LytM/M23 family endopeptidase PA4404 in P. aeruginosa, which we have named LmdC. We have discovered that LmdC is auto catalytically cleaved into N- and C-terminal domains that are then degraded by the carboxyl-terminal processing proteases Prc and CtpA respectively. The effects of various mutations on LmdC-linked {beta}-lactam resistance suggested that full length LmdC is the functional enzyme, with its auto catalytic cleavage serving only to initiate its proteolytic destruction. The auto catalytic cleavage of LmdC was inhibited by overproducing a polymer-forming cytoskeletal protein bactofilin homolog encoded by PA0664, which we named Baf, and a protein of unknown function encoded by PA0663, which we named Api (auto processing inhibitor). We hypothesize that Baf and Api could promote a location specific role for LmdC. In this scenario, the dangerous potential for any free LmdC to cleave peptidoglycan at the wrong place would be prevented by its immediate auto processing and degradation. The widespread co-occurrence and linkage of lmdC and baf homologs, coupled with conserved features of those LmdC homologs, makes it likely that regulated LmdC auto processing is a widely conserved control mechanism.

papers.title: Cannabinoid receptor 1 activity promotes microbial dysbiosis by stimulating the oxygen-dependent expansion of Enterobacteriaceae
papers.abstract: The endocannabinoid system is comprised of bioactive lipids that signal via cannabinoid receptors, which can modulate barrier and immune functions along the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical studies indicate that endocannabinoid activity is dysregulated in inflammatory bowel diseases. Here, we show that endocannabinoid activity promotes metabolic dysfunction within the colonic mucosa, resulting in microbial dysbiosis and exacerbated colitis. Stimulation of the cannabinoid receptor CB1 resulted in the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae within the gut microbiome, a common feature of inflammation-associated dysbiosis. Preceding this microbial change, CB1 activity induced transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial stress and immune activation within the colonic mucosa. This was followed by a reduction in mucosal ATP production and the induction of aerobic respiration genes in luminal Escherichia coli. Genetic inactivation of aerobic respiration in E. coli limited its proliferation, indicating that CB1 activity stimulates oxygen-dependent Enterobacteriaceae growth. In IBD susceptible mice, endocannabinoid activity promoted mucosal infection by an E. coli pathobiont, which corresponded with elevated pro-inflammatory markers. In inflammation resistant mice, acute CB1 stimulation was sufficient to accelerate the infection dynamics of an Enterobacteriaceae pathogen, resulting in exacerbated colitis. Taken together, our data support a model in which endocannabinoid signaling at the CB1 receptor disrupts respiratory metabolism in the colon, compromising the anoxic environment of the lumen that is critical for maintaining aerobically respiring pathogens at low abundance. More broadly, our findings highlight a proinflammatory effect of endocannabinoid activity that can contribute to intestinal disease development.

papers.title: Context-dependent regulation of RpoS-dependent and RpoS-independent gene transcription by Crl during exponential growth in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: RpoS, an alternative sigma factor, directly regulates approximately 10% of gene transcription in E. coli. The small protein Crl functions as a partner that assists RpoS in exerting its regulatory role, particularly during the stationary phase. However, the coordinating role of Crl during the exponential phase remains unclear. In addition, whether Crl can regulate gene transcription independently of RpoS is still unknown. Therefore, in this study, we used the RpoS-dependent operon hdeAB and the RpoS-independent operon proVWX as model systems to investigate the transcriptional regulatory function of Crl using RT-qPCR and 3C-qPCR. Since the expression of both Crl and RpoS is modulated by environmental signals, we further examined the transcription of these operons under different pH and osmotic conditions. The results showed that Crl can regulate transcription independently of RpoS and exhibits environment-specific bidirectional regulation. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of Crl and highlights the complexity of transcriptional regulation.

papers.title: Exploring recurrent urinary tract infection: paired microbiota and culture-based profiling reveals stable dysbiosis and multidrug-resistant, virulence-enriched uropathogens
papers.abstract: **Objectives:** Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) is increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet urinary microbiome dysbiosis and isolate-level resistance-virulence are rarely examined together across different treatment states. In this study, we characterized both within the same sample in rUTI and in healthy controls. **Methods:** In this cross-sectional cohort, mid-stream urine was collected from women with untreated, treated and prophylaxis rUTI and age-matched healthy controls at four centres in South India. Of 80 samples collected, 75 were analysed (26 controls, 20 untreated, 20 treated, 9 prophylaxis) by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing. In addition, 105 culturable isolates from the same samples were identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility (VITEK 2) and phenotypic virulence. **Results:** rUTI groups showed approximately half the alpha diversity of controls (median Shannon 1.07-1.18 vs 2.17; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.041). Community structure differed from controls in every rUTI subgroup (PERMANOVA R-squared = 0.091, p = 0.004; pairwise FDR = 0.008) but not among subgroups. Mean Lactobacillus relative abundance fell from 29.2% in controls to <=13.2% in rUTI groups, while Escherichia-Shigella rose from 7.2% to 25.0-43.0%. Control-referenced dysbiosis z-scores were elevated in all rUTI groups (community distance: FDR <= 0.003; uropathogen: Lactobacillus index: FDR < 0.001 for treated and prophylaxis groups). Among isolates, Escherichia coli predominated (35/105; 16/35, 45.7% multidrug-resistant), followed by Klebsiella spp. (32% multidrug-resistant); carbapenem susceptibility was largely retained, and multidrug-resistant E. coli co-carried more virulence traits. **Conclusions:** rUTI is associated with a stable dysbiotic state that treatment does not restore, combining Lactobacillus loss and uropathogen dominance with a multidrug-resistant culturable reservoir that co-accumulates virulence traits. Reading the community and its isolates together may support microbiome-sparing, resistance-aware management of rUTI.

papers.title: TFA-defluorinating microbial consortium achieved with analogue enrichment
papers.abstract: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is an ultra-short chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and a pollutant of global significance; it is persistent and ubiquitous in the environment across compartments, including food, drinking water, animals, and humans. Concentrations in the environment are rising, concerns over the toxicity of the compound are increasing, and there are currently no efficient ways to remediate TFA pollution, as conventional methods are ineffective at scale under environmental conditions. Microorganisms possessing dehalogenating enzymes targeting the structurally analogous compound monofluoroacetate (MFA) present a potential solution to degrade TFA microbiologically. Due to previously demonstrated dehalogenation of difluoroacetate (DFA) by dehalogenases, the promiscuity of such enzymes was hypothesized to be extendable to TFA as well. In this study cultures obtained from an environmental sample of PFAS contaminated wastewater sludge were incubated in M9 minimal media supplied with 33 mM acetate and either 33 mM TFA, DFA, or MFA in an iterative manner, followed by testing in a 30-day experiment. Free fluoride (F-) was measured at 5 timepoints using a fluoride ion specific electrode (ISE). One culture designated MFA1C significantly degraded MFA, DFA, and TFA (two-way ANOVA mixed model, p < 0.05). MFA1C released 11.2 {+/-} 0.7 M F- which constitutes approximately 0.01% of the potential fluoride release from the total 33 mM TFA applied and with the greatest defluorination activity in the first 9 days of incubation. Fluoride release from TFA and formation of DFA and MFA was confirmed with 19F-NMR. Genetic sequencing and protein-ligand modelling identified two candidate dehalogenase enzymes from Achromobacter denitrificans and Stenotrophomonas sp., respectively, with potential capacity to degrade TFA. The findings of this study are a crucial first step towards future potential bioremediation of TFA, and are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to identify a TFA-degrading consortium of microorganisms.

papers.title: A simple platform for in situ DNA-PAINT optimization enables improved multiplexed super-resolution imaging in Gram-negative bacteria
papers.abstract: DNA-PAINT enables super-resolution imaging with high multiplexing capacity, yet it is rarely used in nanoscale bacteriology. A likely reason is the lack of straightforward protocols and of systematic characterization of imager-docking strand pairs inside intact bacterial cells, whose envelope and dense cytoplasm differ markedly from both the DNA origami in vitro systems used to develop them, and eukaryotic cells. In this work, we establish a screening platform based on RNA-FISH, in which we extend the 16S rRNA-directed EUB338 probe with docking sequences of choice. This allows imager-docking pairs to be benchmarked directly inside Escherichia coli cells and characterized for parameters such as specificity, binding kinetics, and localization precision. We screened 12 different DNA-PAINT sequences and used an optimized set to perform four-target 3D Exchange-PAINT in single E. coli cells. We further applied our strategy to image three effector mRNAs in the Gram-negative pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and quantified RNA clusters and their 3D distribution. Our work provides a framework and practical guidelines for high-quality 3D DNA-PAINT imaging in Gram-negative bacteria and should facilitate its broader adoption in nanoscale bacteriology.

papers.title: Assessment of antimicrobial potential of cell-free supernatant from Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vaginal microbiota of healthy women against uropathogens
papers.abstract: Among women, urinary tract infection (UTI) represents a major health concern. Approximately 50% of the adult female population experienced an episode of UTI at least once. UTI and recurrent UTIs caused by resistant bacteria are very common in clinical settings. The treatment and management of UTI is becoming more challenging because of the rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Lactobacillus spp are the dominant bacterial genus in urinary and vaginal microbiota, which are also used as probiotics. In this study, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vagina of healthy women were evaluated for its probiotic-associated properties and cell-free supernatant (CFS)-mediated antibacterial activity against eight uropathogens. The antibacterial activity of CFS was concentration- and pH-dependent, which was significantly evident at CFS/2 and CFS/4 concentrations and acidic pH values of 4 and 5. The antibacterial activity in CFS remains unaltered even after heat and proteinase K treatment, which suggests the role of heat- and protease-resistant metabolites beside the contributions from acidic conditions. L. paracasei SRG showed strong autoaggregation (85.32%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity (55.60%). In addition, it also exhibits co-aggregation with all indicator strains, suggesting substantial interaction with diverse pathogenic bacteria. These observations highlighted the L. paracasei SRG as a potential probiotic candidate developed from indigenous vaginal microbiota.

papers.title: Single-cell-resolved natural giant virus infections reveal conserved protist immunity
papers.abstract: Single-cell eukaryotes (protists) are key players in microbial ecosystems. Yet, our understanding of how they interact with viruses in nature and how antiviral defenses shape these relationships remains limited. Using a single-cell multi-omics approach, we mapped associations between giant viruses and their hosts and identified active giant-virus infections in an alpine lake protist community. In naturally infected dinoflagellates, infection was accompanied by the selective induction of viperin, an ancient antiviral enzyme conserved from bacteria to humans. We also observed virus-encoded homologs of immunity-related genes whose expression correlated with viperin expression, raising the possibility of a role in viral counter-defense. These findings reveal an ecological dimension of protist immunity and provide a framework for tracing the host-virus arms race across divergent cellular lineages.

papers.title: Glyphosate exposure minimally alters the Corbicula fluminea microbiome while associated bacteria exhibit high tolerance and degradation potentia
papers.abstract: Glyphosate (GLY), the active ingredient in Roundup, is a broad-spectrum herbicide widely used in commercial agriculture and residential landscaping. Due to its extensive application and high water solubility, GLY is frequently introduced into freshwater ecosystems where it has been shown to negatively impact aquatic life and beneficial microorganisms. The freshwater clam Corbicula fluminea, a nonnative bivalve species widely distributed throughout the United States, is highly tolerant of many environmental stressors and may serve as a reservoir for microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading environmental pollutants. As efficient filter-feeders, these clams are continuously exposed to waterborne contaminants, potentially facilitating interactions between pollutants and host-associated microbial communities. In this study, we investigated how glyphosate impacts the structure and diversity of Corbicula fluminea microbiomes and characterized GLY tolerance and degradation potential in individual microbiome members. We found that microbiome taxonomic composition and abundance-based diversity metrics were minimally impacted by glyphosate, while presence/absence-based phylogenetic diversity shifted depending on treatment concentration. Furthermore, high GLY concentrations were linked to reduced Faith''s PD alpha diversity, while other alpha diversity metrics were not impacted. Additionally, we isolated and characterized glyphosate-tolerant bacterial strains from clam tissues and assessed their presence within the microbiome. Several isolates exhibited tolerance to very high GLY levels (up to 1600 mg/L), and several also utilized GLY as a sole phosphorus source and possessed the phnJ gene, suggesting potential degradation capabilities. While isolated bacteria were minority members of the microbiome, more abundant uncultured taxa were phylogenetically related to known glyphosate degraders. Collectively, these findings suggest that freshwater bivalves may harbor diverse microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading herbicides, which may contribute to host resilience in contaminated freshwater environments and potentially represent unexplored avenues for bioremediation research.

papers.title: Sister species, shared and divergent responses: early transcriptomic profiling of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus exposed to Esteya spp.
papers.abstract: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) responds transcriptionally to nematophagous fungi, but the earliest events preceding cuticle penetration are poorly characterized, and whether closely related fungal antagonists elicit comparable responses is unknown. Here, we compared PWN transcriptomic responses to Esteya floridanum V14639 (EF) and E. vermicola CCF3117 (EV) at 1 h post-inoculation (hpi), capturing the onset of host-fungus interaction. Despite their phylogenetic proximity, under our exposure conditions the two fungi elicited partly divergent host responses at 1 hpi. EF induced a broad transcriptional response enriched in peptidase activity and lysosomal pathways, accompanied by downregulation of cuticle structural components. In contrast, EV triggered a narrower response, without the proteolytic and lysosomal enrichment observed with EF. Direct comparison of the two treatments revealed no significantly enriched Gene Ontology categories, although pathway analysis identified DNA replication and repair pathways, comprising genes more highly expressed under EF. Enrichment analyses revealed a shared transcriptional signature in both interactions characterized by downregulation of xenobiotic- and central carbon-metabolism pathways, suggesting an early reduction in xenobiotic detoxification capacity rather than induction of detoxification programs. These findings suggest that phylogenetic proximity does not necessarily predict conserved early transcriptional responses, although comparisons of single isolates cannot separate species-level from isolate-level effects.

papers.title: Interdependent mode of RNA recognition by the interacting KH-domain proteins KhpA and KhpB
papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are central regulators of gene expression. In bacteria, two KH domain-containing proteins, KhpA and KhpB, are increasingly recognized as globally-acting RBPs, including in pathogens that lack well-studied RBPs, such as Hfq and ProQ. While KhpA and KhpB interact with various RNAs in diverse bacteria, their crosstalk and molecular basis of RNA recognition remain poorly understood. Here, we explored the mutual dependence between KhpA and KhpB in the food-borne pathogen Campylobacter jejuni. We demonstrate KhpA and KhpB interact in vivo, and their individual global RNA recognition is largely dependent on the presence of the partner protein. Using RNA co-immunoprecipitation, we reveal that KhpA requires a conserved KH domain motif for RNA binding, whereas KhpB relies on an atypical R3H domain. Moreover, mutating the RNA-binding domain of one protein compromises the RNA interactome of the other. Overall, we demonstrate an interdependent RNA-binding mode of KhpA and KhpB and anticipate that such KH-proteins have co-evolved to elicit joint RNA regulation in bacteria.

papers.title: Mechanistic prediction of fecal microbiota transplant engraftment and Clostridioides difficile colonization resistance with μODE
papers.abstract: Shotgun metagenomics routinely resolves microbial community composition down to the strain level via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), but translating these static catalogs into mechanistic, time-resolved understandings of ecosystem dynamics remains a critical computational bottleneck. Here, we present muODE, a fully automated framework that converts MAGs into dynamical simulations of community metabolism equipped with a composable, literature-grounded ecology layer, fundamentally designed to serve as a mechanistic hypothesis-testing engine. It employs dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) coupled to a shared extracellular pool and integrates a composable ecology layer capturing pH inhibition, time-varying antibiotic pharmacokinetics, bile-acid transformations, and spore dormancy. To evaluate the core engine, we cross-validated the dFBA machinery to machine precision against an independent reference implementation. We provide native export to the established COMETS engine for third-party verification. Benchmarking against two independent experimentally validated datasets confirmed that while monoculture growth is robustly captured, overflow secretion and directed community composition remain strictly bounded by the flux-routing limitations of max-biomass FBA. However, when applied to rate-modifying ecological feedback, muODE mechanistically and quantitatively reproduces bile-acid-mediated colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile. With a single rate parameter calibrated so that baseline deoxycholate matched its measured physiological concentration, the framework reproduced the uncalibrated antibiotic-induced collapse of deoxycholate, with the calibrated inhibitor concentration coinciding with the independently set inhibitory threshold of the pathogen and driving a ~44x shift in the simulated pathogen-susceptibility ratio; bile-acid transformation is represented in the composable ecology layer rather than in the genome-scale stoichiometry. Finally, applying muODE end-to-end to a real longitudinal fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) yielding 139 de novo genome-scale metabolic models, the framework successfully recovered the clinical direction of treatment. By transparently diagnosing the structural competitive-exclusion bias that limits precise compositional prediction, muODE motivates the necessity of community-objective extensions while transitioning microbiome modeling from descriptive taxonomy toward testable, quantitatively-validated dynamic hypothesis testing, laying the essential mechanistic groundwork for the predictive engineering of safe, targeted ecological therapeutics. muODE is freely available at https://github.com/cumbof/muODE.

papers.title: Mice immunized with N1 neuraminidase in a single cycle infectious virus or in a recombinant nanoparticle vaccine are protected against lethal challenge with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 influenza
papers.abstract: The recent spillover of highly pathogenic (HP) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into dairy cattle and other mammalian species has been concerning. Vaccine candidates that can be rapidly synthesized and implemented are key countermeasures for protecting the human population against emerging pathogens. Here we examine the use of a pH1N1 virus lacking the genetic material for hemagglutinin (HA), limiting the infection to a single cycle (sciIAV) or Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (NA) of HPAI H5N1 (N1-CoPoP) as vaccine candidates. C57BL/6 mice that were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV did not differ in serum NA antibody compared to uninoculated mice. However, mice that were inoculated intramuscularly with the N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies. Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all mice inoculated with either pH1N1 sciIAV or N1-CoPoP were protected from weight loss, unlike unvaccinated mice with substantial body weight losses that succumb to viral infection between 7 and 10 days post infection (dpi). Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP immunization minimized viral infection such that only one mouse receiving pH1N1 sciIAV had detectable viral titer in the lungs at 4 dpi. By 6 dpi, no mouse inoculated with pH1N1 sciIAV and/or N1-CoPoP had detectable virus in nasal turbinates, lungs or the brain, unlike the high viral titers found in uninoculated mice. Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP were protective and should be investigated further as alternative vaccine candidates.

papers.title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
papers.abstract: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.

papers.title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.

papers.title: Distribution and dynamics of Vibrio spp. and pathogen sequences among microhabitats and monsoon seasons in Singapore's coastal waters
papers.abstract: Marine infections are rising in temperate regions due in part to a warming climate. However, comparatively little is known about drivers of marine pathogen dynamics in the tropics where temperatures are high year-round. Vibrio bacteria are ubiquitous in both temperate and tropical marine environments, and many are important pathogens of marine organisms and humans. Here, we sampled an equatorial monsoonal site, the Singapore Strait, over 18 months and applied amplicon sequencing (16s rRNA V6-8 region) to three particle size fractions, qPCR quantitation of Vibrio spp., and generalized linear modelling with environmental variables to understand the factors that structure the Vibrio assemblage. We found that Vibrios represented the highest proportion of pathogen-related DNA sequences, with an assemblage composition influenced by microhabitats (size fractions) and monsoon seasons. Vibrio sequences were dominated by ASVs with highest identity to V. xuii, V. rotiferianus and V. caribbeanicus, and including ASVs matching agents of human disease in Singapore - V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus, and V. furnissii. Vibrio qPCR abundance was lowest in the largest size fraction (10-150 m), following planktonic DNA trends, even though pathogen-related sequences, including Vibrio, were enriched in this fraction. Temperature was a significant predictor of overall Vibrio abundance, but its effect was no longer significant after adjustment for monsoons, suggesting that the temperature association may reflect broader seasonal dynamics. Instead, effects of chlorophyll, ammonia, nitrate and suspended solids were more consistent within seasons. Furthermore, free-living and particle-associated Vibrios responded differently to environmental changes, suggesting that partitioning into microspatial habitats may lead to differences in their environmental sensitivity.

papers.title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
papers.abstract: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.

papers.title: Pulling water from a stone: subaerial biofilm water dynamics on porous solid materials
papers.abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) are microbial communities that colonize air exposed surfaces in both natural and engineered environments, forming an interface between the atmosphere and the substrate. Often water availability is crucial for their metabolic activity and survival. While precipitation may contribute to SAB hydration, the dynamic processes of evaporation and condensation - closely linked to fluctuating temperature and humidity conditions - can be key determinants of water availability and they constitute the main focus of this study. We present a model connecting the water-related dynamics in an SAB, its surrounding ambient air and underlying stone/masonry. A central feature of the model is the increased water affinity of the SAB in comparison to the stone pore network. Based on thermodynamic principles, the model captures changes in liquid water content and availability by accounting for the evaporation and condensation at liquid-gas interfaces through gradients in water chemical potential. It accounts for the SAB's capacity to delay water loss by drawing water from substrate material pores to compensate for atmospheric evaporation. The proposed model is compared to prior experimental observations of water transport in limestone samples with and without SAB. Additional numerical simulations under variable environmental conditions demonstrate how permeability of the substrate layer may influence SAB water activity, and how the presence or absence of an SAB might affect water content within stone/masonry.

papers.title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from Escherichia coli identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
papers.abstract: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.
